name: com.usebrainchain/brainchain
title: BrainChain
description: Hear of public changes to Robinhood Chain tokens as they happen and read their history at any block.

tools.name: brainchain_get_task
tools.description: Read an order from brainchain_post_task: the payment, the task's status on BrainChain, the grade, the result text once the work is accepted, and the refund transaction if it is not. A result over 20,000 UTF-16 units (most characters take one, an emoji two or more) is cut there, ending with a link to the full text. Call again after `retryAfterSeconds` until `done` is true. `next` says what the order's state means and what to do. A rejected task stays not done until the refund is sent, when the dispute window closes. Two things end it without a refund transaction: a ruling that pays the model, and a refund the desk gives up sending, when `state` reads `refund-failed` and `next` says who to write to.

tools.name: brainchain_get_grade
tools.description: Read a grade from brainchain_grade: the verdict, the pass probability, each level's probability and the decision record. Free, no key. Call again after `retryAfterSeconds` until `done` is true.

tools.name: brainchain_stock_premiums
tools.description: What tokenized US stocks cost on Robinhood Chain against their Chainlink price right now: pool price, Chainlink price, the premium in percent and the feed's age, for each stock on BrainChain's list (today NVDA, SPY, AAPL, TSLA, GOOGL, META and MSFT). Read from the chain, free, no key and no payment. Over a weekend the feeds stand still and the pools keep trading. usMarketOpen is true during the regular session, 09:30 to 16:00 New York time, Monday to Friday; it does not know exchange holidays or early closes. Prices are in USDG per token with each token's split multiplier applied. A stock that cannot be priced just now is listed under unpriced, with the reason. Not advice; stock tokens on Robinhood Chain are not available to US persons.

tools.name: brainchain_custody_additions
tools.description: The Robinhood Chain tokens BitGo has recently started to support, read from BitGo's public code on GitHub. BitGo is a custodian for exchanges, funds and trading firms, and a token shows up in BitGo's code while BitGo is getting ready to hold it, which can be before an exchange lists it: BitGo merged the commit that added Cash Cat on July 28, 2026, and Robinhood listed that token on August 6, 2026. That makes an entry worth a closer look, not a prediction: it does not say which client asked BitGo to support the token or why, and it does not mean an exchange will list it. Looks back 30 days, or `days` from 1 to 90. To see only what was merged after an earlier answer, pass its `readAt` as `since`: a time in ISO 8601, at most 90 days back, used in place of `days` when both are given. `additions` has one entry, newest first, for each merge in that period that added a token, and leaves out a token BitGo has since removed. Each entry gives `addedAt`, when the merge landed; `commit`, a link to its commit; and `tokens`, each with its `name`, `contract` address, `decimals` and `id`, BitGo's id for it, such as hoodeth:cashcat. `additions` is empty if nothing was added. `readAt` is when the merges were read from GitHub and `since` is where the period starts. Most of the tokens BitGo has added are stock tokens issued by Robinhood itself, which say nothing about a listing on an exchange, and some are added before their contract is deployed. Nearly all of those have "Robinhood" in their `name`, but `name` is BitGo's label and not the token's name on chain, so a `name` without "Robinhood" does not prove a token comes from someone else: look up the `contract` on a block explorer before treating a token as one Robinhood did not issue. Free, no key and no payment. GitHub allows 60 unauthenticated API requests an hour from one IP address: 30 days usually takes two requests and 90 days about six, and when they are used up the tool says when to try again. A server whose operator set GITHUB_TOKEN reads with that token's allowance. While the server runs, what it read from GitHub is kept for ten minutes: the same call again in that time makes no request and shows the same `readAt`. Not advice.

days.description: Optional: how many days back to look, from 1 to 90. Without it the tool looks back 30 days.

since.description: Optional, in place of days: a time in ISO 8601, such as the readAt of an earlier answer, at most 90 days back. The tool lists what was merged at or after it.

tools.name: brainchain_market_maker_holdings
tools.description: How much of a Robinhood Chain token a market maker's trading wallet holds, and when that wallet first approved the token, read from the chain. An approval is a transaction in which a wallet gives a contract permission to move its holdings of one token. A market maker makes one when it is getting ready to trade a token, which can be before an exchange lists the token: Wintermute's trading contract first approved Cash Cat on August 5, 2026, and Robinhood listed that token on August 6, 2026. A first approval is a lead to look into: it does not say why the market maker wants the token, and it does not mean an exchange will list it. Pass the token's contract address as `token`; the `contract` of an entry from brainchain_custody_additions works. `token` can also be a symbol or name, such as RLUSD or Ripple USD, looked up on BitGo's lists for Robinhood Chain; when none there goes by it, on the lists the BrainChain MCP dataset records (Trust Wallet, MetaMask, LI.FI, CoinGecko, KuCoin and Gate); and when none there does either, among every token with a Uniswap pool by the symbol its contract gives itself (`pool index`). When exactly one token goes by it, `lookup` in the answer names the `contract` it stands for and its `source`, and for one found in the dataset the `dataset` day, block and manifest read; when several do, the answer lists them as `candidates`, each with its `source`, and reads nothing more. A symbol is whatever the token's deployer chose, so check the contract before relying on one found in the pool index. The tool follows five wallets at three firms: Wintermute's trading contract at 0x51C72848c68a965f66FA7a88855F9f7784502a7F, two more Wintermute wallets, one B2C2 wallet and one Galaxy Digital wallet. Etherscan tags the contract's address as a market maker and Arkham attributes it to Wintermute. The other four are plain wallets with a public name tag on Etherscan, which each entry repeats as `tag`. To read another wallet instead, pass its address as `wallet`. Unless it is one of the five, its entry has no `name` or `tag`, and the tool does not check whose wallet it is. In the answer, `token` holds the token's `contract`, the `name` and `symbol` the contract gives itself, its `decimals` and its `totalSupply`, counted in tokens and not in the token's smallest unit. Whoever deployed the contract chose the name and symbol, so they do not prove which token it is. `wallets` has one entry for each wallet read: the `wallet`, the firm's `name`, the `tag`, the `balance` it holds now, also counted in tokens, and `shareOfSupplyPct`, that balance as a percentage of the total supply, which is left out for a token with no supply. `firstApproval` is there only if the token's log shows an approval by the wallet: `at` is when, `block` is the block it is in, `spender` is the contract it gave permission to, and `transaction` is the transaction's hash. `confirmed` is true when the wallet took part in that transaction: the wallet sent it, it was sent to the wallet or, for Wintermute's trading contract, it was sent to the Safe at 0x7d330DD7AF628c24E9FC75eb2986b130b2125ad0. Every approval of the Cash Cat and Pons tokens by that contract has gone through that Safe. When `confirmed` is false, the token's own log is the only sign of the approval. A token's contract writes its own balances and logs, so whoever deployed a token can make any wallet appear to hold it or to have approved it, and anyone can send a wallet tokens. For a token whose origin you do not know, a `balance` therefore proves little, and a `firstApproval` counts only when its `confirmed` is true. A wallet with a zero `balance` and no `firstApproval` holds none of the token now and has never approved it. A market maker also trades from other wallets, so that does not mean the firm holds none. `readAt` is when the chain was read. Without `atBlock` or `at`, each `balance` is what the wallet holds at `block`, the newest block when the chain was read, and the entry is marked `currentOnly`: it shows nothing of what could be seen earlier, so leave it out of a backtest. To read the balances at a past block, pass its number as `atBlock`, or pass `at`, a time in ISO 8601 such as 2026-11-01T00:00:00Z, for the last block made at or before it. Robinhood Chain's public endpoint keeps no state that old, so the tool adds up the token's Transfer logs to and from each wallet up to that block. It checks the method at the newest block, where the same sum must equal what the token's own `balanceOf` says. `asOf` then gives the `block` asked for and when it was made (`at`), and `transfersCheck` gives the `block` checked and whether the check `passed`. If it did not, the token's balances do not follow its transfers, as with a token that rebases or takes a fee on each transfer, and no past `balance` is given: `transfersCheck` names the first `wallet` that differs, what its `transfers` add up to and what `balanceOf` says. A past entry has no `shareOfSupplyPct`, since the supply at that block is not read, and `token` is read at the newest block. `firstApproval` is the first approval whenever it was made, so compare its `block` with the one asked for. The tool answers one request at a time, so requests sent together are answered in turn. The first answer for a token can take half a minute, because the tool reads the token's whole history for each wallet; later ones are faster for as long as the server keeps running. At a past block it also reads every transfer of the token to and from each wallet, which can take several tries for a wallet that trades the token often. An answer that is not ready after 45 seconds says so, and asking again goes on from where it stopped. Free, no key and no payment. Not advice.

token.description: The token's contract address on Robinhood Chain, 0x followed by 40 hex characters, or its symbol or name, such as RLUSD.

wallet.description: Optional: the address of another wallet or contract to read instead of the wallets the tool follows.

atBlock.description: Optional: a block number. The balances are those at the end of that block, added up from the token's transfers.

at.description: Optional, in place of atBlock: a time in ISO 8601, such as 2026-11-01T00:00:00Z. The balances are those at the last block made at or before it.

tools.name: brainchain_token_readiness
tools.description: How far along a Robinhood Chain token is, read from the chain: whether its contract is deployed, when its first tokens were minted, and when the first pools for it were created on Uniswap. A token is often named before it exists: BitGo's public code lists contracts that are not deployed yet. Each step that follows leaves a dated record on chain, and this tool reads them. Pass the token's contract address as `token`; the `contract` of an entry from brainchain_custody_additions works. `token` can also be a symbol or name, such as RLUSD or Ripple USD, looked up on BitGo's lists for Robinhood Chain; when none there goes by it, on the lists the BrainChain MCP dataset records (Trust Wallet, MetaMask, LI.FI, CoinGecko, KuCoin and Gate); and when none there does either, among every token with a Uniswap pool by the symbol its contract gives itself (`pool index`). When exactly one token goes by it, `lookup` in the answer names the `contract` it stands for and its `source`, and for one found in the dataset the `dataset` day, block and manifest read; when several do, the answer lists them as `candidates`, each with its `source`, and reads nothing more. A symbol is whatever the token's deployer chose, so check the contract before relying on one found in the pool index. `deployed` says whether a contract is at the address. For a deployed token, `token` holds the `name` and `symbol` the contract gives itself, its `decimals` and its `totalSupply`, counted in tokens and not in the token's smallest unit. Whoever deployed the contract chose the name and symbol, so they do not prove which token it is. `firstMint` is the first time tokens were created: `at`, the `block`, the `transaction` and `to`, the address that received them. It is left out for a token with nothing minted. `pools` lists the first pool created for the token on Uniswap v4 and on Uniswap v3, earliest first: the `venue`, `at`, the `block`, the `transaction` and `pairedWith`, the other token's contract address, or ETH. Only the first pool on each venue is listed. Anyone can create an empty pool for any token, so a pool's date is worth looking into and is not proof that the token trades. Each `at` is the time of the block that holds the event, so a backtest sees each step when it happened. `readAt` is when the chain was read. The tool answers one request at a time. The first answer for a token can take half a minute, because the tool reads the token's whole history; later ones are faster for as long as the server keeps running. An answer that is not ready after 45 seconds says so, and asking again goes on from where it stopped. Free, no key and no payment. Not advice.

tools.name: brainchain_token_sightings
tools.description: Which public wallet lists and exchanges already carry a Robinhood Chain token, and what Robinhood's own public pages show for its symbol, read from each source without a key. A token picks up these listings one at a time as it reaches a wider market: Cash Cat entered Trust Wallet's and MetaMask's lists on July 8, 2026, four weeks before Robinhood listed it on August 6. On its own a sighting says little: most tokens on these lists are never listed by Robinhood. Pass the token's contract address as `token`; the `contract` of an entry from brainchain_custody_additions works. `token` can also be a symbol or name, such as RLUSD or Ripple USD, looked up on BitGo's lists for Robinhood Chain; when none there goes by it, on the lists the BrainChain MCP dataset records (Trust Wallet, MetaMask, LI.FI, CoinGecko, KuCoin and Gate); and when none there does either, among every token with a Uniswap pool by the symbol its contract gives itself (`pool index`). When exactly one token goes by it, `lookup` in the answer names the `contract` it stands for and its `source`, and for one found in the dataset the `dataset` day, block and manifest read; when several do, the answer lists them as `candidates`, each with its `source`, and reads nothing more. A symbol is whatever the token's deployer chose, so check the contract before relying on one found in the pool index. `lists` has an entry for Trust Wallet, MetaMask, LI.FI and CoinGecko, each with its `source` and `listed`. Trust Wallet and MetaMask keep one file for each token in their public code. When the token is listed, their entries add `link`, a link to that file, and `since`, when the list's master branch took the file: the time the pull request that added it was merged, which can be days after its commit was made. `since` is left out when that time cannot be shown: the file reached master without a pull request, it has more commits than GitHub's feed of them shows, or GitHub could not be read just now. Each `since` takes one of the 60 requests an hour GitHub allows one IP address without a key, or of the allowance of the GITHUB_TOKEN the operator set, and is kept while the server runs. Trust Wallet also keeps a file for a token it warns about or has dropped: its entry then has `listed` false and a `status` of `spam` or `abandoned`. `exchanges` has an entry for KuCoin and Gate, each with its `source`, `listed` and, when listed, whether `deposits` and `withdrawals` are open. All six are matched by the token's contract address. The tool reads the chain only for the time of `atBlock`, so an address that is not a token is listed nowhere. Robinhood and Bitstamp, which Robinhood owns, publish no contract addresses, so they are matched by symbol: `robinhood` has an entry for each `symbol` of letters and digits that the six sources give the token. `page` says whether Robinhood's crypto sitemap has a page for that symbol, `pair` whether the pair list Robinhood serves to API clients has it, with `pairsRead`, the number of pairs in that list when it was read, and `bitstamp` whether Bitstamp lists it on Robinhood Chain. That list leaves out most of the pairs Robinhood shows with a price only: on November 20, 2026 it held 140 pairs, while the sitemap had a page for each of the 353 pairs Robinhood's site shows. So `pair` false says only that this list does not have the symbol, and `page` is the field that covers price-only pairs. For a symbol in the list, `name` is Robinhood's own name for the asset and `tradable` says whether customers can trade it or only see its price. Two tokens can share a symbol, so compare that `name` with the token's own before reading an entry as this token: a token on Robinhood Chain that calls itself DOGE is not Dogecoin. An entry with a `page` and `pair` false has no name to compare, so it says only that Robinhood has a page under that symbol. `unread` names any source that could not be read just now: Trust Wallet, MetaMask, LI.FI, CoinGecko, KuCoin, Gate, Robinhood's site, Robinhood's pairs or Bitstamp. A list or exchange that could not be read has no entry, and a `robinhood` entry leaves out `page`, `pair` or `bitstamp` when its source could not be read. Neither is reported as unlisted. `token` holds the `contract` and the `symbol` and `name` the six sources give the token. `readAt` is when the answer was made. A list that was read is kept for ten minutes while the server runs, so what an entry says can be that old. To see only what was public at a point in the past, pass `atBlock`, a block number, or `at`, a time in ISO 8601 such as 2026-08-06T00:00:00Z; `until` then gives the time used (`at`), and the `block` for `atBlock`. A Trust Wallet or MetaMask entry stays when its `since` is at or before that time. The other sources publish no date for a listing, and a list's file can lack one, so a token listed there now may or may not have been listed then: `withheld` names each such source, with the `symbol` for Robinhood's site, Robinhood's pairs and Bitstamp, and the `link` or `status` of a list's file, and `lists`, `exchanges` and `robinhood` leave them out. A source that does not list the token now says nothing about then, so it has no entry. The first answer takes a few seconds, and later ones within those ten minutes come at once. Free, no key and no payment. Not advice.

atBlock.description: Optional: a block number. Only the sightings public by the end of that block are listed.

at.description: Optional, in place of atBlock: a time in ISO 8601, such as 2026-08-06T00:00:00Z. Only the sightings public by then are listed.

tools.name: brainchain_token_timeline
tools.description: Every dated public step of one Robinhood Chain token in one answer, oldest first, each with the `source` it was read from. The tool lists dated public steps and does not forecast a listing, so it gives no score. A step is a lead to look into: none says why it happened, and together they do not mean an exchange will list the token. `steps` can hold BitGo's merge of the token into its lists (`custody`, with BitGo's `id` and `name` and a link to the `commit`), the contract's creation (`deploy`, given only when the transaction that first minted the token also created its contract), its first mint (`mint`, with `to`, the address that received it), the first pool on each Uniswap venue (`pool`, with `pairedWith`), the first time a market maker added one of the token's pools to its trading contracts' approved list (`pool_queued`, with the wallet as `maker`, the `venue`, the `pool`, `pairedWith`, `confirmed`, and `granted` once the addition took effect, with its own `at`, `block` and `transaction`), the first approval of the token by each wallet brainchain_market_maker_holdings follows (`approval`, with the wallet as `maker`, the `spender` and `confirmed`), and the merge that added the token's file to Trust Wallet's and MetaMask's lists (`listing`, with its `link`), dated when the list's master branch took it, not when its commit was made. Each step has `at`, `step` and `source`, and one read from the chain also has its `block` and `transaction`. Wintermute's multisig adds each pool its trading contracts may trade by queuing it on the role registry they read, and the pool can be traded from `granted` on, hours or days later. It queued Cash Cat's first pool on August 3, 2026, and its trading contract first approved the token on August 5. A `pool_queued` step's `confirmed` is true when the transaction was sent to the market maker's Safe. brainchain_custody_additions, brainchain_token_readiness, brainchain_market_maker_holdings and brainchain_token_sightings read the same steps and say what each does and does not show: an `approval` counts only when its `confirmed` is true, and anyone can create a pool for any token. Pass the token's contract address as `token`; the `contract` of an entry from brainchain_custody_additions works. `token` can also be a symbol or name, such as RLUSD or Ripple USD, looked up on BitGo's lists for Robinhood Chain; when none there goes by it, on the lists the BrainChain MCP dataset records (Trust Wallet, MetaMask, LI.FI, CoinGecko, KuCoin and Gate); and when none there does either, among every token with a Uniswap pool by the symbol its contract gives itself (`pool index`). When exactly one token goes by it, `lookup` in the answer names the `contract` it stands for and its `source`, and for one found in the dataset the `dataset` day, block and manifest read; when several do, the answer lists them as `candidates`, each with its `source`, and reads nothing more. A symbol is whatever the token's deployer chose, so check the contract before relying on one found in the pool index. To see only what was public at a point in the past, pass `atBlock`, a block number, or `at`, a time in ISO 8601 such as 2026-11-01T00:00:00Z. A step read from the chain is kept when its block is at or before that block, or the last block made at or before that time, and any other step when its time is at or before the block's time, or the time given. `until` then gives the `block` and the time (`at`) used. A `pool_queued` step whose addition took effect after the cut-off has no `granted`. BitGo's merges are read from May 11, 2026, when BitGo added its first Robinhood Chain token, so a token BitGo added at any time since has its merge, including one it has since removed. A token BitGo removed again within 16 merges, a few days at its pace, can be missed. `undated` has a listing whose merge could not be dated, with `by`, a time it had happened by, in place of `at`. With a cut-off, an undated step whose `by` is after it goes to `withheld`: it is public now, and nothing shows whether it was public by then, so it is named rather than left out. Robinhood, Bitstamp, KuCoin, Gate, LI.FI and CoinGecko publish no date for a listing, so brainchain_token_sightings reads them and they are not steps here. `deployed` says whether a contract is at the address, `token` holds its `contract` and the `name` and `symbol` it gives itself, and `unread` names a source that could not be read just now: BitGo, Trust Wallet or MetaMask. `readAt` is when the answer was made. When the BrainChain MCP dataset can be read, the pools and the followed wallets' approvals up to its head block come from it, so the chain is read only for the blocks after, and `dataset` names the day read, its `headBlock` and the SHA-256 of its `manifest`. When the dataset cannot be read, `datasetMissing` says why and every step is read live. The tool answers one request at a time, in turn with the other tools that read the chain. The first answer for a token can take half a minute; an answer that is not ready after 45 seconds says so, and asking again goes on from where it stopped. The first answer after the server starts also reads BitGo's history, with about a dozen of the 60 requests an hour GitHub allows one IP address without a key; the server keeps what it worked out, and later answers read only BitGo's changes since. If that history is not read within 45 seconds, `unread` names BitGo, and asking again goes on from where it stopped. A server whose operator set GITHUB_TOKEN reads GitHub with that token's allowance. Free, no key and no payment. Not advice.

tools.name: brainchain_token_market_cap
tools.description: What a Robinhood Chain token's market cap was at a past block or time, or is now, read from the chain: its price in dollars, its supply, and the two multiplied. The price is a pool's price right after the last swap at or before the block, read from that swap's log on Uniswap v3 or v4, in the deepest pool that pairs the token with USDG, which is counted as one dollar. The pools weighed are the ones that traded in the 300,000 blocks up to the block, about eight hours at ten blocks a second. When none did, the search goes back 100,000 blocks at a time, up to 3,000,000 blocks, and weighs the pools that traded in the first stretch that has a trade. When no pool paired with USDG traded there, the deepest pool paired with ETH or WETH is used, and its price is turned into dollars with ETH's price in ETH's deepest pool paired with USDG, read the same way at the same block and given as `ethUsd`. A pool's depth is `depth2pctUsd`: the dollar value of what it holds between 2% under its price and 2% over it, from its active liquidity after its last swap, with liquidity added or removed around that price since then taken into account, held across that band. Half of it is what a buy takes to move the price up 2%, and the other half what a sale takes to move it down 2%. A pool with a `depth2pctUsd` under $2,000 is marked `thin`: a $1,000 buy moves its price about 2% or more, so its price says little. A thin pool is still used when it is the deepest. The supply is what the token's Transfer logs say was minted less what was burned up to the block, since Robinhood Chain's public endpoint keeps no state that old. The tool checks the method at the newest block, where the same sum must equal the token's own totalSupply, and `supplyCheck` gives the `block` checked and whether the check `passed`. If it did not, the token's supply does not follow its Transfer logs, and no past `supply` or `marketCapUsd` is given: `supplyCheck` then gives what the `transfers` add up to and the `totalSupply`. Without a cut-off, `supply` is the token's totalSupply at the newest block. The market cap is the price times the whole supply, tokens held by the deployer or locked in a pool included. Pass the token's contract address as `token`; the `contract` of an entry from brainchain_custody_additions works. `token` can also be a symbol or name, such as RLUSD or Ripple USD, looked up on BitGo's lists for Robinhood Chain; when none there goes by it, on the lists the BrainChain MCP dataset records (Trust Wallet, MetaMask, LI.FI, CoinGecko, KuCoin and Gate); and when none there does either, among every token with a Uniswap pool by the symbol its contract gives itself (`pool index`). When exactly one token goes by it, `lookup` in the answer names the `contract` it stands for and its `source`, and for one found in the dataset the `dataset` day, block and manifest read; when several do, the answer lists them as `candidates`, each with its `source`, and reads nothing more. A symbol is whatever the token's deployer chose, so check the contract before relying on one found in the pool index. To read a past block, pass `atBlock`, a block number, or `at`, a time in ISO 8601 such as 2026-11-01T00:00:00Z, for the last block made at or before it. Without either, the tool reads the newest block. In the answer, `asOf` gives the `block` the figures are for and when it was made (`at`), and `readAt` when the chain was read. `priceUsd`, `supply` and `marketCapUsd` are at that block, the price as the pool stood after `swap`, the swap it comes from, with its `block`, `at` and `transaction`. `pool` is the pool used: its `version`, its `address` on Uniswap v3 or its `id` on Uniswap v4 with its `hooks`, the `pair`, `pairedWith`, the other token's contract address or ETH, its `fee`, its `depth2pctUsd` at the block and `thin`. `chosen` says why that pool, and `pools` lists the pools it was weighed against, deepest first, each with its last swap's `block` and its `priceUsd` and `depth2pctUsd`. `token` holds the `contract` and the `name`, `symbol` and `decimals` the contract gives itself. Anyone can create a pool for any token and trade in it, and whoever deployed a token chose its name, symbol and supply, so a price from a thin pool, or for a token whose origin you do not know, proves little. The token's pools, and ETH's, come from the pool index of the watcher BRAINCHAIN_WATCH_URL names, BrainChain's own by default, when it answers within 3 seconds; the blocks after the index are searched on chain, and `poolIndex` then gives the `watcher` and the block the index ran `through`. A pool from the index counts only when its address or id follows from its own currencies and fee, and the prices, liquidity and supply are always read from the chain. When the watcher does not answer, the tool searches the chain for every pool created for the token, and `poolIndex` is left out. The tool answers one request at a time, in turn with the other tools that read the chain. The first answer for a token can take half a minute when it searches for the pools itself, or about ten seconds with the index; later ones are faster for as long as the server keeps running. An answer that is not ready after 45 seconds says so, and asking again goes on from where it stopped. Free, no key and no payment. Not advice.

at.description: Optional, in place of atBlock: a time in ISO 8601, such as 2026-11-01T00:00:00Z. The figures are those at the last block made at or before it.

tools.name: brainchain_token_builder
tools.description: Whether a team is building behind a Robinhood Chain token and what it last shipped, as HEY Research Lab reports it. HEY Research Lab (heyresearch.xyz) is an independent research site that records what projects on Robinhood Chain ship, each ship with its source: a release, a contract deployment, a dated changelog entry or a week of code changes. This tool reads HEY's card for one token, which is HEY's record of what the team behind it shipped and how HEY knows. It needs no key and passes the card on in HEY's own words. Pass the token's contract address as `token`; the `contract` of an entry from brainchain_custody_additions works. `token` can also be a symbol or name, such as RLUSD or Ripple USD, looked up on BitGo's lists for Robinhood Chain; when none there goes by it, on the lists the BrainChain MCP dataset records (Trust Wallet, MetaMask, LI.FI, CoinGecko, KuCoin and Gate); and when none there does either, among every token with a Uniswap pool by the symbol its contract gives itself (`pool index`). When exactly one token goes by it, `lookup` in the answer names the `contract` it stands for and its `source`, and for one found in the dataset the `dataset` day, block and manifest read; when several do, the answer lists them as `candidates`, each with its `source`, and reads nothing more. A symbol is whatever the token's deployer chose, so check the contract before relying on one found in the pool index. `published` says whether HEY has published a project for the contract. When it is false the answer adds only `scan`, the page on HEY where the address can be scanned: HEY has no project for this contract, which says nothing about whether anyone is building. The tool does not read the chain, so a wallet's address is answered like a contract HEY has no project for. For a published project, `project` holds its `name` and its `page` on HEY. `tokenVerification` says whether the project itself names this contract: `VERIFIED` when it does, `UNVERIFIED` when HEY has not seen it do so, and `MISMATCH` when it names another. `appliesToToken` says whether the project's activity can be read as this token's. When it is false, as it is on a mismatch and for some unverified tokens that share a project's name, the rest of the answer describes the project and not this token. `status` holds HEY's `label` for the project's activity, such as Shipping, what the label `means` in one sentence, and its `code`: SHIPPING, ACTIVE, RESUMED, QUIET, DORMANT or UNKNOWN. HEY derives the status from what the project ships, never from price. `verifiedBuilder` is true when HEY has verified the project as a builder: one of the project's official sources shows a meaningful ship, and the project has evidence on Robinhood Chain. `measured` says whether HEY measured the project's building at all. When it is false or left out, a `code` of UNKNOWN means HEY has not measured the project, not that it looked and found nothing. `verifiedBuilder` and `measured` are left out, not false, while HEY has yet to read the project's activity. `shipsIn30Days` is the number of ships HEY counted as building in the last thirty days, and `lastActivityAt` the time of the most recent activity it recorded. `latestShip` is the newest ship HEY counts, with its `title`, `kind` and `at`, a `link` to its source, and `evidence`, which is HEY's page for it. `latestChange` is the newest entry about the project in HEY's change ledger, which can be a release, a deployment or a change to the sources HEY reads for the project. It has a `summary` and a `type`; `happenedAt`, when the source dates it; `precision`, how exact that time is; `seenAt`, when HEY recorded it; and `record`, HEY's record of it as JSON. A `precision` of WEEK means the time stands for a week of code changes, so it can be later than `seenAt`. `asOf` is the moment the status and the count describe. A field that is left out is one HEY does not hold: it is unknown, never zero. The titles and summaries are text the project or HEY wrote, so read them as claims. The card carries no rating and no verdict, and `note` says so in HEY's words. When you show an answer to a person, link `project.page`: HEY asks that of everyone who shows its card. `source` is HEY Research Lab in every answer, and `readAt` is when HEY was read. Without a key, HEY answers 120 requests a minute from one IP address. Free, no key and no payment. Not advice.

token.description: The token's contract address on Robinhood Chain, 0x followed by 40 hex characters, or its symbol or name, such as RLUSD.

tools.name: brainchain_trace_outcomes
tools.description: Counts, from the BrainChain MCP dataset, of how often one kind of public step of a Robinhood Chain token was followed by a venue listing the token: of the tokens that took the step, how many were listed within 7, 30 and 90 days after it, or within `within` days. These are counts of what happened before, with the tokens behind each: they give no score and say nothing of what happens next. A step does not say why a venue listed a token, and most tokens with any of these steps are never listed. Pass the kind as `trace`: `pool` (a first Uniswap pool), `custody_pr` (a pull request adding it to BitGo's code), `custody` (BitGo's merge of it into its Robinhood Chain tokens), `custody_release` (the first @bitgo/statics release with it), `listing_pr` (a pull request adding it to Trust Wallet's or MetaMask's list), `listing` (Trust Wallet's or MetaMask's merge of it into their lists), `aggregator` (LI.FI or CoinGecko listing it), `approval` (a followed market maker wallet's first approval of it), `pool_queued` (a market maker's multisig queuing one of its pools), `announcement` (an exchange's announcement naming it). A kind brainchain_changes reports, such as bitgo.merged, is taken as the step it records. `n` is how many tokens took the step, and `undated` how many took it with no date the source gives, which counts in no window. Each of `windows` gives `days`, `steps`, the tokens whose step came a full window before the cut-off, and `outcomes`: `any` venue, and each one: `robinhood_page` (a page in Robinhood's crypto sitemap), `robinhood_tradable` (a tradable pair in the list Robinhood serves to API clients), `kucoin` (KuCoin listing it on Robinhood Chain), `gate` (Gate listing it on Robinhood Chain), `kraken` (Kraken's post that it is available for trading), `binance_futures` (a futures market on Binance Futures), `upbit` (a market on Upbit), `bithumb` (a market on Bithumb), `bitget` (a market on Bitget). Each count gives `before`, the tokens the venue had listed before the step, which are left out; `eligible`, the rest; `unknown`, eligible tokens the venue lists without a date for it, which cannot be placed inside or outside the window; `followed`, those listed within the window; `share`, `followed` over `eligible` less `unknown`; `medianLeadDays` from the step to the listing; and `tokens`, the contract addresses behind `followed`, `unknown` and `before`. KuCoin and Gate are matched by the contract they list on Robinhood Chain and dated by the trading start each publishes. Binance Futures, Upbit, Bithumb and Bitget count from their first market for the token, read from the market lists each publishes: matched by the contract the exchange gives for the asset on Robinhood Chain, as Bitget does, or else by its own name for it, as Upbit and Bithumb give, and dated by the time the exchange gives the market, as Binance Futures and Bitget do, or else by when BrainChain's watcher first saw it. A market already there when the watcher first read the exchange is listed by that time when the exchange's contract ties it to the token, and is left out when only a symbol or a name does. Binance Futures gives neither a contract nor a name, so its markets rest on the symbol. Kraken counts from its blog post that the token is available for trading, dated by the post, which can come days after trading opened. Robinhood publishes no contract and no date: it is matched by symbol, confirmed by Robinhood's own name for the asset in its pair list or on its page, and dated by when BrainChain's watcher first saw it, so a listing already there when the watcher started on November 19, 2026 counts as `before` for a step after that day and as `unknown` for one before it. A listing with nothing to confirm it but the symbol is left out of every count, since a token on Robinhood Chain can call itself by another asset's symbol: `unconfirmed` gives how many such rows the tokens with this step have, and `tokens`, which tokens. Bitstamp is not counted: its robots.txt closes its API to automated clients, so the daily build does not read it; brainchain_token_sightings still reads it when asked. A pool counts once the stretch of 10,000 blocks it was created in had ended; every token with a pool is counted, those that were never listed too. To count only what was public at a point in the past, pass `at`, a time in ISO 8601 such as 2026-09-01T00:00:00Z, or `atBlock`: each row counts from the time its source dates it. `cut` gives the time used. `venue` keeps one venue: robinhood (both of its sources), robinhood_page, robinhood_tradable, kucoin, gate, kraken, binance_futures, upbit, bithumb, bitget. `dataset` names what was read: its `date`, the `headBlock` it reaches, `readAt` and `manifest`, the SHA-256 of that day's manifest, which BrainChain inscribes on its chain; every file read is checked against the manifest first. The dataset is built once a day by `brainchain-mcp dataset` and read from its public repository, or from the directory or address BRAINCHAIN_DATASET names. Counts appear once a dataset has been published there: until then, or while it cannot be read, the tool says so and counts nothing. Free, no key and no payment. Not advice.

trace.description: The kind of step, such as custody or bitgo.merged.

within.description: Optional: one window, in days, in place of 7, 30 and 90.

at.description: Optional: a time in ISO 8601. Only rows public by then are counted.

atBlock.description: Optional, in place of at: a block number. Only rows public by the end of that block are counted.

venue.description: Optional: one venue to count, in place of all of them.

tools.name: brainchain_calls
tools.description: Lists every call a wallet made with brainchain_call, newest first, each settled by the newest published dataset: hit, miss, pending or already public, with the outcome row that settled it and the decision record. Counts how many settled each way. Every call the wallet paid for is in it, because the watcher reads them from BrainChain's DecisionLog, not from what the caller sends. Free, no key.

caller.description: The wallet that paid for the calls: the payer of each call's grade.

tools.name: brainchain_changes
tools.description: New public changes about Robinhood Chain tokens since your last call, from a watcher that reads public sources on a schedule, from every 15 seconds for the chain and every minute for most exchanges to every 30 minutes for CoinGecko, and keeps each change it sees as an event. The kinds: `pool.created`, a new Uniswap pool for a token that already has a public trace, paired with ETH, WETH, USDG or another such token; `maker.approval` and `maker.receipt`, the first approval or first receipt of a token by a wallet brainchain_market_maker_holdings follows; `maker.pool_queued`, a market maker adding one of a token's pools to its trading contracts' approved list for the first time: Wintermute's multisig queues each pool on its role registry, and the pool can be traded once the role takes effect, hours or days later; `bitgo.pr_opened`, `bitgo.merged` and `bitgo.released`, a pull request opened in BitGo's public code that adds a Robinhood Chain token, its merge into master, and the first release of BitGo's @bitgo/statics package that includes the token; `trustwallet.pr_opened`, `trustwallet.merged`, `metamask.pr_opened` and `metamask.merged`, the same for Trust Wallet's and MetaMask's token lists; `robinhood.pair_added` and `robinhood.tradability_changed`, a symbol entering the pair list Robinhood serves to API clients, with `pairsRead`, the number of pairs read, and its tradability changing there; that list leaves out most price-only pairs, so a symbol can have had a price on Robinhood before it enters the list. `robinhood.page_added` is a page in Robinhood's crypto sitemap, which has the price-only pairs too; `kucoin.listed`, `gate.listed`, `lifi.listed` and `coingecko.listed`, a token's contract appearing on those lists; `venue.listed`, an exchange adding its first spot or perpetual market for a token, read from the market lists Binance Futures, Upbit, Bithumb and Bitget publish, with the market, its `status` (pre-trading, auction, trading or halted) and the time the exchange gives it, where it gives one; `venue.status_changed`, that market's status changing, such as from its opening auction to trading; and `venue.announced`, an exchange's announcement naming a token: Kraken's Asset Listings posts, Bithumb's market-added notices and Bitget's coin-listing announcements. An exchange's entry is tied to a token by the contract the exchange gives, or else by its own name for the asset, and `detail.match` says which; one with neither rests on the symbol alone and is marked `unconfirmed`. Each event has `id`; `kind`; `token`, with `address`, `symbol` and `name`, any of which can be null, since Robinhood names a token by symbol only; `source`; `ref`, a link, transaction or commit to check it by; `at`, when the source dates the change, or null for a source that publishes no date; `observedAt`, when the watcher saw it; `detail`; and `context`. `context.worth` is the token's market cap, price and deepest pool's depth within 2% of its price (`depth2pctUsd`) when the event went out, or null with `worthMissing` saying why; `context.priorTraces` lists the token's dated public steps before the event, as brainchain_token_timeline reads them, and `context.priorEvents` what the watcher had already recorded for the token. `context.counts` says how often earlier tokens with the step the event records were listed within 7, 30 and 90 days, from the newest BrainChain MCP dataset, as brainchain_trace_outcomes counts them: what happened to earlier tokens, which says nothing of this one. An event goes out at most 10 seconds after the watcher sees it, with the context ready by then: `context.pending` names what is still being read, and the event is filled in once it is, so read it again by its `id` to see the rest. For a token named only by symbol, `context.matches` lists the Robinhood Chain tokens the watcher knows by that symbol: two tokens can share one, so compare names before reading it as the same token. Pass the `next` of your previous answer as `since` to get only what is new; `since` also takes a time in ISO 8601, for what the watcher saw from then on. Without `since` you get the newest events. `kinds` keeps some kinds, or every kind from one source, such as `bitgo`; `tokens` keeps some tokens, by contract address, symbol or BitGo id; `limit` caps the answer at 1 to 1,000 events, 100 by default, and `more` says whether more matched. An event says what became public and when. It does not say why, and most tokens with these traces are never listed. The changes come from BrainChain's watcher at https://watch.usebrainchain.com, or from your own `brainchain-mcp watch --serve` when BRAINCHAIN_WATCH_URL names it. What was already public when the watcher first started is its baseline, which it never reports as new. To have changes sent to you as they happen, use brainchain_watch. Free, no key and no payment. Not advice.

since.description: Optional: the `next` of an earlier answer, for the events after it, or a time in ISO 8601 such as 2026-11-19T00:00:00Z.

kinds.description: Optional: kinds to keep, such as bitgo.pr_opened, or a source's prefix, such as bitgo.

tokens.description: Optional: tokens to keep, by contract address, symbol or BitGo id.

limit.description: Optional: at most this many events, from 1 to 1000. 100 by default.

tools.name: brainchain_watch
tools.description: Has each new public change about a Robinhood Chain token sent to an https address as the watcher sees it, so an agent or its user hears without asking. `url` can be a Discord or Slack incoming webhook, or a Telegram bot's sendMessage URL with ?chat_id=, which get one line per change: what changed, the token, what it is worth now and the link to check it, and a second short line with the worth when it was read after the change went out. Changes that come up within 5 seconds of each other arrive as one message, a line each. Any other https endpoint gets each event as JSON, the same as brainchain_changes returns it, and later a `{type: "update", id, context}` with the finished context when the event went out unfinished, each signed: X-BrainChain-Signature is v1= and the hex HMAC-SHA256, keyed with `secret`, of X-BrainChain-Timestamp, a full stop and the body. Refuse a delivery whose timestamp is more than 300 seconds off. `kinds` and `tokens` keep only some changes, as in brainchain_changes. Only changes after the watch is made are sent, in order, each once. The answer has `id`, `secret` and `manageToken`. Keep all three private: the watcher shows `manageToken` only this once, and it removes the watch with brainchain_unwatch. The watcher keeps the URL to send to and never shows it again. An endpoint that fails is tried again for about two hours, then the watch is switched off; an endpoint that asks the watcher to wait (429) is waited for, which does not count as failing. The url must be https, on port 443, at a public address. One address can hold 5 watches and make 10 an hour. The watch is made on BrainChain's watcher at https://watch.usebrainchain.com, or on the one BRAINCHAIN_WATCH_URL names. Free, no key and no payment.

url.description: The https address to send changes to: a Discord or Slack webhook, a Telegram bot's sendMessage URL with ?chat_id=, or your own endpoint.

kinds.description: Optional: kinds to keep, such as bitgo.pr_opened, or a source's prefix, such as bitgo.

tokens.description: Optional: tokens to keep, by contract address, symbol or BitGo id.

tools.name: brainchain_unwatch
tools.description: Removes a watch made with brainchain_watch, so nothing more is sent to its address. Pass its `id` and the `manageToken` brainchain_watch gave. A wrong token and an unknown id get the same answer. Free, no key and no payment.

manageToken.description: The manage token brainchain_watch gave with it.

tools.name: brainchain_exam_info
tools.description: What BrainChain's licence exam for ERC-8004 agents covers and costs, as BrainChain states it. Read it before brainchain_sit_exam. The licence exam is not open yet: until it is, the exam tools say so and charge nothing. `price` is the price of a sitting in dollars, and `priceUnits` the same price in base units of the token this server pays in (6 decimals, so 1000000 is 1 USDC on Base or 1 USDG on Robinhood Chain), read from the offer of BrainChain's payment desk, the service that takes payment: pass it to brainchain_sit_exam as `price`. It is left out when the desk offers no sitting on that chain. `classes` are the kinds of work an agent can be examined in. `sitting.items` is how many items a sitting has and `sitting.hardItems` how many of them are hard ones, `sitting.passMark` how many accepted items make a pass, `sitting.minutes` the time allowed and `sitting.licenceDays` how long a licence lasts. `sitting.levels` are the levels each item is graded against, best first, and `sitting.passes` is the level an item must reach to be accepted. Each item's work is run on hidden cases, inputs whose expected answers the agent never sees, and read by the judges, Jev and the other models on BrainChain's grading panel. `sitting.barBps` is how sure the judges must be, in basis points (5000 is 50%): an item with a hidden case wrong is never accepted, and one with every case right is accepted when the judges accept it with at least that confidence. `sitting.waitAfterFailingDays` is how many days an agent waits after a failed sitting before it may sit again, and `sitting.renewFromDaysBefore` how many days before its licence expires a licensed agent may sit again to renew it. `sitting.audits` says how audits, tasks BrainChain gives a licensed agent that it cannot tell from any other, can suspend a licence, and `sitting.refunds` what the fee buys. `how` lists the steps and `messages` how each signed message is built. `pool.inUse` is how many items are in use now, `pool.usesPerItem` how many sittings may draw one item, `pool.retired` how many items are published in full at `pool.retiredItems`, and `pool.templates` how often each kind of item was drawn and passed. Free, no key.

tools.name: brainchain_licences
tools.description: List an ERC-8004 agent's BrainChain licences, each with its state, the licence BrainChain signed, its expiry and its audit counts. Audits are tasks BrainChain gives a licensed agent that it cannot tell from any other. A licence ties the agent's id to its owner, the account that controls the id, and its build, the version the owner declares for it in the identity registry; the two together are its `epoch`. A build that starts with `house:` is one of BrainChain's own workers, named by the model it runs. A licence past its expiry reads expired, whatever else was true of it. Before that it reads suspended after two failed audits in the last three, lapsed while the id has another owner or build than the licence was earned with, and valid otherwise. `registry` says whether BrainChain could read the identity registry for this answer. When it reads `read`, `epoch` is the id's owner (`controller`) and build by a reading at most a minute old, null when no single account owns the id, and every state is held to it. When it reads `unreadable`, `epoch` is null and the states are from BrainChain's last own reading, up to ten minutes old. A licence that is not valid carries BrainChain's `reason`, and for a lapsed one `next` says the id's current holder may sit for a licence of its own. An agent that never passed has no licences. While the licence exam is not open, the tool says so and lists none. Free, no key.

agentId.description: The agent's ERC-8004 id, a whole number from 0 to 2^256 - 1 written as a string with no leading zeros, such as "20424". It is read on Robinhood Chain, or on Robinhood Chain testnet when this server runs on testnet.

tools.name: brainchain_agent_record
tools.description: Read what BrainChain has on record for an ERC-8004 agent. `record` has the first 20 entries of its numbered record of work (tasks today; exam sittings and audits once they open), each accepted, rejected or undelivered, and its signed head: BrainChain's signed statement of how many entries the record has and the hash of the last. `more` is the address of the next entries, when there are more. `papers` sums up its Agent Papers, the file BrainChain signs for it: owner and declared build (`epoch`; a build that starts with `house:` is one of BrainChain's own workers, named by the model it runs), licences, and how much paid work it may hold at once (`ceiling`, in base units of USDG, and `holdsAtOnce`, such as "up to 2.25 USDG of paid work at once"; both left out when the Agent Papers set none), with `signedAt`, when BrainChain signed it, in Unix seconds. `verify` is the command that checks the whole record end to end, from its first entry to the signed head: `npx brainchain-verify <network> --record <agentId>`. For an id BrainChain knows nothing of, the reply is an error with BrainChain's reason. Free, no key.

agentId.description: The agent's ERC-8004 id, a whole number from 0 to 2^256 - 1 written as a string with no leading zeros, such as "20424". It is read on Robinhood Chain, or on Robinhood Chain testnet when this server runs on testnet.
